items.stem: You add `public int Grade { get; set; }` to a POCO. It compiles and runs, but some Grade changes never sync to the destination. What rule did you break?

options.text: Synnduit POCO properties must be nullable; a bare non-nullable int breaks change detection
Grade must be a string
Every property needs a [DuplicationKey]
POCOs cannot have integer properties at all

items.explanation: Synnduit requires properties to be nullable. A non-nullable int prevents the engine from reliably detecting changes, so updates are silently missed.

misconceptions.b: The type doesn't need to become a string — it needs to become nullable (int?) or use a nullable proxy.
misconceptions.d: Integers are fine; they just need to be nullable (int?).

items.stem: Why does Synnduit require POCO properties to be nullable?

options.text: To save database space
So the engine can represent 'no value' and tell it apart from a real default (0, false), which change detection depends on
Because EF cannot map non-nullable types
To make every field optional in the UI

items.explanation: The nullable distinction lets the engine separate 'absent' from a legitimate default value, which is what reliable change detection needs.

misconceptions.c: EF maps non-nullable types fine; this is a Synnduit change-detection requirement, not an EF limitation.

items.stem: You need a property to stay non-nullable (`int EnrollmentStatus`) for the destination, but satisfy Synnduit's nullable rule. What is the correct pattern?

options.text: Mark it [Required] and hope for the best
Add a [NotMapped] nullable proxy property and wire it via [EntityProperty(NullableProxyProperty = nameof(...))]
Change it to a string
Remove the [EntityProperty] attribute

items.explanation: The nullable-proxy pattern keeps the non-nullable property but routes the engine through a [NotMapped] nullable proxy linked by the NullableProxyProperty annotation.

misconceptions.d: Removing [EntityProperty] would stop tracking the field entirely — the opposite of what you want.

items.stem: When using the nullable-proxy pattern, where does the feed's Map method assign the incoming source value?

options.text: To the non-nullable property directly
To the nullable proxy property; Synnduit moves it to the non-nullable one internally via the annotation
To both properties manually
It doesn't — the engine reads the database column directly

items.explanation: You assign to the nullable proxy (e.g. c.NullableEnrollmentStatus = reader.GetInt32(11)); the engine propagates it to the non-nullable property through the NullableProxyProperty link.

items.stem: Why is the non-nullable-property bug especially dangerous, and what do you see in the console after applying the fix and re-running in test?
rubric: Dangerous because it is silent: no compile error and no exception — it appears to work, but some changes are never picked up
After the fix, re-running shows the engine reconciling the affected records, with NoChangesMerged entries counted in the console as it corrects them
items.sampleAnswer: It's dangerous because nothing fails loudly — the code compiles and runs, so you assume it works, while certain field changes silently never sync. After switching to nullable (or the proxy pattern) and re-running in test, the console shows the correction progressing, with NoChangesMerged entries as it reconciles the previously-missed records.

items.stem: Your `SourceSystemEntityId` is composed from non-nullable value-typed source fields (e.g. `int StudentNumber`, `int PersonId`). What is the recommended way to satisfy the nullable rule for the identifier?

options.text: Give SourceSystemEntityId a plain getter/setter and build the string directly in the feed's Map (e.g. string.Format("{0}_{1}", ...)) from the source fields
Add a [NotMapped] nullable proxy for the string SourceSystemEntityId itself
Make SourceSystemEntityId an int? so it can represent 'no value'
Nothing is needed — identifier fields are exempt from all nullable handling, including their source fields

items.explanation: The SourceSystemEntityId property is itself a string (a nullable reference type), so it needs no proxy. Because it's assigned explicitly by composing the source fields in Map, the value is set directly rather than diffed through the engine, so the nullable-proxy plumbing isn't required on it.

misconceptions.b: The string property is already a nullable reference type; a proxy is for non-nullable value types, not for the identifier string.
misconceptions.c: SourceSystemEntityId is a string identifier, not an integer — it isn't retyped to int?.
misconceptions.d: The identifier string is exempt, but its underlying non-nullable value-typed source fields still follow the nullable rule; the direct-assignment approach is what lets you avoid a proxy per field.

items.stem: A POCO is fed by two sources (PowerSchool and a JSON feed), each providing only a subset of its properties. By default, when the JSON feed doesn't supply a property and it arrives as null, what does the engine do with that null?

options.text: Treats it as 'not part of this sync' and leaves the existing value unchanged
Overwrites the existing value with null
Throws an exception because the property is required
Deletes the destination record

items.explanation: By default a source's null on a property it doesn't provide is ignored — it isn't a change. This is a core reason properties are nullable: it lets the engine tell 'this source didn't supply a value' apart from a real change, so one source doesn't blank out fields owned by another.

misconceptions.b: That's what [ForceNullPropagation] makes it do for a specific named source; the default is to ignore the null.
misconceptions.c: A subset feed legitimately leaves other properties null; that isn't an error.

items.stem: You want a null coming from PowerSchool to actually overwrite the previous value (set it to null), while a JSON feed that provides only a subset should keep having its nulls ignored for that same property. What do you put on the property?

options.text: [ForceNullPropagation(typeof(PowerSchool.PowerSchool))] — propagates PowerSchool's null as a change, and applies only to PowerSchool
[ForceNullPropagation] on the property with no source type, so every source's null propagates
[Required] on the property
Remove [EntityProperty] so nulls are always written

items.explanation: ForceNullPropagation names one source system: a null from that source is applied as a change (value → null) instead of ignored. Because it's scoped to PowerSchool, the JSON feed's nulls for that property keep the default 'ignore' behavior.

misconceptions.b: The point is source-specific propagation; naming PowerSchool is what leaves the JSON feed's nulls ignored.
misconceptions.c: [Required] is about validation, not null-change semantics.
misconceptions.d: Removing [EntityProperty] stops tracking the field for change detection entirely — the opposite of what you want.
